mcqs.question: Why is mobile-first (min-width media queries) generally preferred over desktop-first (max-width media queries)?
options: Because max-width queries are not supported in older browsers
Because mobile-first requires fewer total CSS rules regardless of layout complexity
Because it's the default recommended by the CSS specification itself
Because the simpler small-screen layout becomes the base case, so weaker devices don't have to download and override desktop-only rules first
mcqs.explanation: Mobile-first avoids shipping unused desktop styles to constrained devices that then have to be overridden, since the lean base case is the default and complexity is added only as space increases. Both max-width and min-width queries are equally well supported, and the spec itself doesn't mandate either direction.

mcqs.question: Why is font-size set purely in `vw` considered an accessibility issue?
options: vw units are not supported by screen readers at all
vw scales with the viewport but ignores the user's browser zoom or OS text-size preference, unlike rem
vw always renders smaller than the equivalent px value
vw cannot be combined with any other CSS unit
mcqs.explanation: A user who increased their default font size for readability expects text to respect that, and rem — tied to the root element's font-size — does; pure vw is tied only to viewport width and overrides the user's preference. Screen readers read the underlying text content regardless of the unit used to size it visually.

mcqs.question: A card component looks correct at full page width but cramped when placed inside a narrow sidebar on the exact same viewport. What's the right fix?
options: A container query on the card's wrapper, since the problem is the space the component is given, not the viewport size
A viewport media query with a narrower max-width threshold
Increasing the sidebar's z-index so the card renders at full width
Switching the card's units from rem to vw
mcqs.explanation: The viewport hasn't changed at all in this scenario, so a viewport-based media query can't distinguish the two placements — only a container query, which measures the actual containing box the component sits in, can. Neither z-index nor a unit swap addresses the layout logic at all.

mcqs.question: You need to show a different, tighter crop of a hero photo on narrow screens rather than just a smaller version of the same image. Which technique is built for that?
options: srcset with width descriptors alone
The sizes attribute on a plain img element
<picture> with a <source> element scoped by a media query, for genuine art direction
Increasing the image's resolution and letting CSS scale it down
mcqs.explanation: srcset/sizes solve resolution switching — same crop, different pixel density or size — while <picture> exists specifically for art direction, swapping to an entirely different image or crop based on a condition. Scaling one large image down in CSS wastes bandwidth and doesn't change the crop at all.

mcqs.question: What problem does `clamp(1.75rem, 4vw + 1rem, 3.5rem)` solve that a plain `font-size: 4vw` does not?
options: It removes the need to test on multiple screen sizes entirely
It bounds the fluid size with a floor and ceiling, so text never gets unreadably small or unreasonably large at the extremes
It makes the font-size update only on page load instead of on resize
It converts the vw unit into a fixed pixel value automatically
mcqs.explanation: A raw vw value scales without limit in either direction; clamp() adds the min and max bounds so the fluid middle value only applies between them, while a plain vw font-size can shrink below readable sizes on small viewports. It still updates live on resize and remains a relative unit — clamp just constrains the range.

mcqs.question: A heading uses `font-size: 5vw` and becomes unreadably small on a 320px-wide phone. What's the most robust fix?
options: Wrap the vw value in clamp() with a sensible minimum, e.g. clamp(1.5rem, 5vw, 3rem)
Switch the unit to vh instead of vw
Add !important to force a larger rendered size
Remove the vw unit and hardcode a single px value for every viewport
mcqs.explanation: clamp() keeps the fluid scaling behavior that vw provides while adding a floor that prevents the unreadable-small case — which is the actual bug, not a lack of !important priority. Switching to vh targets the wrong axis entirely, and a single hardcoded px value throws away the fluid scaling the design wants.
